deep.reconstruction:
This is not a Gauss manuscript derivation. It is page 4 of a printed 18th-century German textbook on arithmetic, interleaved in Gauss's copy. The bundle name 'HB.Leiste' and the style point to Christian Leiste's 'Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, 1790). The handwriting at the right edge belongs to the facing interleaved leaf, i.e. the 'next page': bibliographic notes on Euler's papers. Those cover the Euler-integral paper on ∫x^{p-1}(1-x)^{(q-n)/n}dx at x=1, magic squares in the Vlissingen Mémoires, Tome IX 1782, the parallax paper in the Berlin Ephemerides 1783, and the 1766 note on increasing grain yield. They end with a count of 208 papers in manuscript.

Printed content, §3 continued:
- Homogeneous magnitudes (lengths, areas, volumes, weights, values) are measured by a chosen measure, the 'Einheit' (unit).
- If the magnitude is measured exactly by the unit, it is given as an integer. If only a part of the unit fits, it is a fraction ('Bruch') relative to that unit.

Worked example: a segment AB consists of parts AC, CD, DE, EB. With the common measure F:
- DC = 2F
- DE = 3F
- EB = 4F
- AC = 5F

So AB = (5+2+3+4)F = 14F. The text does not state this total; it is my fill-in. Knowing the size of F and the count of F's in AB gives the length of AB as a number. Two things must therefore be known: (1) the size of the unit, and (2) how many times it is contained in the given magnitude.

Definitions that follow:
- Calculating ('Rechnen') is finding, by comparison with known magnitudes of the same kind, the number that determines a magnitude.
- A 'benannte Zahl' is a number with a unit (inches, feet).
- An 'unbenannte Zahl / Ziffer' is a bare count.
- 'Allgemein bestimmte Zahlen' are letters used as general symbols, needed for deriving the rules of arithmetic.

In modern terms, F is a common measure of the four segments. The largest such measure is the gcd: 1 in units of F, since gcd(5,2,3,4)=1.
errors: The text claims that with DC, the smallest part, none of the other parts can be measured. But EB = 4F = 2·DC, so DC does measure EB exactly (twice). It fails only for AC (5F) and DE (3F). The claim should read 'not all of the other parts'. This is a slip in the printed textbook.
Minor: the total AB = 14F is never stated, though it is implied by 'die Anzahl aller gleich großen Theile in AB'.

results.what: Definition of unit, integer and fraction as the result of measuring a magnitude; segment example with common measure F (AC:CD:DE:EB = 5:2:3:4).
results.modern_name: Measurement by a common unit (Euclidean commensurability / common measure)
results.usually_credited_to: Euclid, Elements Books V, VII and X; standard 18th-century textbook material (e.g. Wolff, Kästner, Leiste)

results.what: Distinction between named and unnamed numbers and use of letters as general numbers.
results.modern_name: Concrete vs abstract numbers; literal (algebraic) notation
results.usually_credited_to: Standard school arithmetic; letter notation from Viète (1591)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is printed elementary textbook text (Leiste) defining unit, fraction and named/unnamed numbers. Gauss's only trace here is the cut-off handwriting belonging to the facing leaf, which is a bibliographic list of Euler's papers. There is no mathematics by Gauss on this page.

checkable.asserts: F is the greatest common measure of the four parts (in units of F)
EB (4F) is an exact multiple of DC (2F), contradicting the text's claim that DC measures none of the other parts
DC does not measure AC or DE

transcription_corrections: The handwritten margin text at the right edge belongs to the facing interleaved manuscript leaf (the 'next page'), not to this printed page. Read with that leaf, it is: 'Observationes circa integralia...', 'Memoires [de la Société de Vlissingue] Tome IX 1782', 'Ephem[erides de Berlin]', 'Memoir[es ...] VI. 1766', and 'Anzahl 208 ... im zweiten ... Novis act[is]'.
The margin line 'Ange 208' should read 'Anzahl 208' or 'Anz.d 208', consistent with the next-page transcription.
Figure labels from top to bottom are B, E, D, C, A on a ticked vertical line, with a short separate segment labelled F (marked with a small 'I') to the right.
There is a faint bleed-through or stamp 'Auf' near the end of the line 'in AB) enthalten sey'. It is not part of the text.
